purpose: Iron sucrose is used to treat iron deficiency anemia, especially in people with chronic kidney disease who are on dialysis or not on dialysis. It helps your body have enough iron to make healthy red blood cells. Your doctor may also prescribe it if you cannot absorb iron from pills or if oral iron has not worked well for you.
how_it_works: Your body needs iron to make hemoglobin, which is the part of your red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout your body. Iron sucrose delivers iron directly into your bloodstream through an IV, so it bypasses your stomach and gets absorbed right away. This helps your body build up its iron stores and produce more healthy red blood cells.
common_side_effects: Some people experience nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach cramps. You might also notice headache, dizziness, muscle cramps, or low blood pressure during or after the infusion. Some people get mild swelling, redness, or a burning sensation at the injection site. These effects are usually temporary and go away on their own.
warnings: Rarely, iron sucrose can cause a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis, which may include difficulty breathing, chest tightness, swelling of the face, or a sudden drop in blood pressure. Tell your healthcare team right away if you feel unwell during your infusion. Let your doctor know if you have any allergies, liver disease, or infections, as these may affect whether this medication is safe for you. This medication is given in a medical setting so staff can monitor you closely.
typical_dosing: Iron sucrose is given as an IV infusion or slow injection at a clinic, hospital, or dialysis center — you will not give it to yourself at home. The dose and how often you receive it depends on your specific condition, your iron levels, and whether you are on dialysis. A common dose for dialysis patients is 100 mg given during each dialysis session for several sessions. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
